source.title_on_document: Designing Human and Generative AI Collaboration

supplement.where: Supporting Information occupies PDF pp. 17-57 (separately numbered SI pp. 1-41). PDF p. 17 also lists an MDAR Reproducibility Checklist as other supporting material; that checklist is not included in this PDF.
supplement.holds: Study design, recruitment, instructions, surveys, rating rubrics, regression specifications, Figure S1, and Tables S1-S12. Table S4 (PDF p. 48) supplies coefficients and standard errors for originality, interestingness, writing quality, and coherence; Table S7 (PDF p. 51) supplies overall-quality coefficients and standard errors. Tables S8-S9 (PDF pp. 52-53) give skill-heterogeneity analyses. No separate table or stated interval/test procedure for content-diversity results was found.

paper_design_summary: Students in an elective emerging-technologies course wrote without AI on Day 1 and with ChatGPT 3.5 on Day 2 under randomly assigned Human Confirmation, Human Creativity, or Copilot rules; raters scored the stories and computed measures assessed genres and similarity across writers (PDF pp. 4, 6-7, 18-21). AI-design comparisons are randomized; comparisons with the earlier no-AI session have a fixed order. An ancillary autonomous ChatGPT-versus-human DAT benchmark reuses the same participants' baseline scores and is retained as a context dataset, not an additional recruited sample or an assistance effect (PDF pp. 8, 11, 35).

assignment.what_was_assigned: Individual students were randomly assigned to one of three Day 2 AI collaboration modes. Everyone first wrote without AI on Day 1; AI availability/order itself was not randomized. This is coded field_rct because the experiment used an exercise within an elective course (PDF pp. 4, 18).
assignment.quote: Participants were randomly assigned to one of three AI collaboration models:
assignment.locator: PDF p. 4, Theoretical Background and Experimental Design; PDF p. 20 (SI p. 4), Figure S1.

arms.name: Human Confirmation
arms.description: Day 2, T1 (Group B in instructions): ChatGPT performs ideation, outlining, drafting, and editing; students prompt, accept/reject, or request regeneration, and may not introduce their own ideas (PDF pp. 4, 18, 26-27).

arms.name: Human Creativity
arms.description: Day 2, T2 (Group A in instructions): students ideate and outline without AI; ChatGPT drafts and edits. During production students prompt and accept/reject output but may not introduce additional ideas or directly write/edit (PDF pp. 4, 18-19, 28-29).

arms.name: Copilot
arms.description: Day 2, T3 (Group C in instructions): students and ChatGPT collaborate iteratively at every stage; students may provide ideas, write, edit, and request suggestions or feedback (PDF pp. 4, 19, 30-31). Copilot is the unrestricted comparator for Atlas coding; the paper does not designate a default and its regressions use Human Confirmation as the reference.

arms.name: Writing without AI (Day 1)
arms.description: All students first write a story manually without AI. This is the shared, fixed-order baseline, not a separately randomized arm or an after-AI assessment (PDF pp. 4, 19-20, 24-25).

participants.exclusions: PDF p. 18 states that all submitted stories were included, including those taking longer than the recommended 105 minutes (7 participants on Day 1 and 3 on Day 2). The paper reports 285 successfully participating students but does not print a distinct analyzed-person total, per-arm people counts, or a participant flow reconciling the missing records. Table 1 (PDF p. 11) has 280 initial-survey/DAT records; PDF p. 21 has 549 stories (278 Day 1, 271 Day 2) and 2,196 ratings. Table 1 also reports 508 exit-survey observations across days and 248 Day 2 AI-support survey records; PDF p. 42 reports reflective feedback from 197 participants. These are different outcome samples; none is relabeled as an overall analyzed-person count. No intention-to-treat claim is made.
participants.who: Students in an elective course on emerging technologies, participating through a classroom exercise with course-credit incentives. The paper reports 285 participants. Four ratings per story came from two fellow participants and two external student research assistants; nine external evaluators were recruited, and are not added to the writer sample (PDF pp. 18-19).
participants.quote: A total of 285 students successfully participated in the experiment.
participants.locator: PDF p. 18 (SI p. 2), A.1 Participants and Participant Recruitment; PDF p. 21 (SI p. 5), A.2 Data and Variables; PDF p. 11, Table 1.

ai_tool.how_used: Students used ChatGPT after prompt-engineering training, with permissions determined by the assigned mode; Copilot allowed free collaboration throughout, while Human Confirmation and Human Creativity restricted human contributions as described in the arms (PDF pp. 4, 18-19, 26-31). GPT-4o was used separately to classify genres (PDF p. 6), and OpenAI text-embedding-3-large to measure semantic similarity (PDF p. 16); these were measurement tools, not the assigned writing assistant.

task.description: Produce a new 1,000-word short story on each of two study days, with any genre allowed. The process comprised ideation, outlining, drafting, and editing, supported by instruction in a seven-sequence narrative structure (PDF pp. 4, 24-33).
task.duration: Main text specifies a 105-minute writing session each day (PDF p. 4); SI recruitment and Figure S1 also specify 105 minutes, with recruitment additionally specifying 15-minute surveys (PDF pp. 18, 20). SI task descriptions instead specify 75 minutes each day (PDF p. 19). The discrepancy is unresolved; the calendar interval between days is not stated.

outcomes.name: Overall story quality
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Each story received four 1-7 ratings from two fellow participants and two external student research assistants, blinded to writer identity and collaboration condition (PDF pp. 19, 21, 41). Primary between-mode regressions use individual evaluations, with DAT, writing experience, writing ability, and English proficiency controls (PDF pp. 23, 44, 48, 51). The paper does not state participant/story clustering or evaluator effects. n_units = 2,196 is the reported total number of evaluations for this metric across both days and all arms (PDF pp. 11, 21), not a Day 2 contrast-specific sample size; regression-specific Ns are unreported. Day 1 comparisons are fixed-order before_after comparisons. Holistic rubric asks whether the story conveys its main ideas creatively, interestingly, coherently, and with good writing (PDF pp. 21, 41). Overall mean 4.91, SD 1.35 across all ratings (PDF p. 11, Table 1); this is not an arm-specific or participant-level SD. Table S7 reports models with and without covariates as robustness variants of this outcome. Skill-heterogeneity analyses are not additional outcomes: Table S8 (PDF p. 52) instead averages ratings to the participant/story level and regresses Day 2 quality on Day 1 quality; adjusted slopes are Human Confirmation 0.0864 (SE 0.114), Human Creativity 0.2442** (SE 0.093), and Copilot 0.2069** (SE 0.095), with ** p < 0.05. Table S9 (PDF p. 53) uses evaluation-level ratings and reports adjusted DAT coefficients 0.0139** (SE 0.006) on Day 1 and -0.0005 (SE 0.006) on Day 2; ** p < 0.05. Figure 2E (PDF p. 13) further displays quality by baseline DAT subgroup. Table S5 (PDF p. 49) models associations of the other four ratings with overall quality, rather than an AI treatment contrast. Overall story quality is a main finding; the other four ratings are called additional quality metrics (PDF pp. 43-44). This is narrative priority, not preregistration.

Content diversity is a main domain, but no priority among its individual genre-composition, genre-similarity, and semantic-similarity measures is stated (PDF pp. 4, 6-7, 15-16, 21).

diversity_detail.metric: Cosine similarity between each story's text embedding and the average embedding of other stories in the same condition.
diversity_detail.computed_over: One similarity value for each story, compared with the mean embedding of all other stories in its condition. Conditions are the three Day 2 collaboration modes and pooled Day 1 writing without AI; these are not all pairwise comparisons (PDF pp. 6-7, 16).
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Condition means and 95% confidence intervals are printed, but the interval calculation and significance-test procedure are not stated. No dependence correction, bootstrap, permutation method, or independent-unit standard error is identified (PDF pp. 6-7, 15-16).
diversity_detail.notes: Higher raw similarity means less diversity. The contrast directions reverse this orientation, while every reported number remains in the paper's original similarity units. No standardized effect or difference was calculated. Before_after comparisons do not isolate AI access from day/order effects.

outcomes.name: Genre similarity between different writers' stories
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: GPT-4o classified each story into one or more of nine literary-fiction genres (PDF p. 6). Cosine similarity then compares a story's nine binary genre indicators with the mean genre vector of other stories in its condition (PDF p. 16, Figure 4B caption). This is categorical-vector similarity, not a count of categories or similarity between text embeddings. The current measure vocabulary supplies no exact type, so measure is null pending an Atlas vocabulary decision; the source calculation is confirmed. Figure 4B shows density plots and condition means with 95% CIs. n_units = 549 is the full analyzed story corpus across both days, not a count of independent pairs or a contrast-specific N (PDF pp. 18, 21). Content diversity is a main domain, but no priority among its individual genre-composition, genre-similarity, and semantic-similarity measures is stated (PDF pp. 4, 6-7, 15-16, 21).

eligibility.reason: S1 meets all three core criteria for the Day 2 ai_design comparisons. The study reports 285 participating students, a one-new-story-per-student Day 2 task, inclusion of all submitted stories in analysis, and 271 Day 2 stories (PDF pp. 18-19, A.1; PDF p. 21, A.2). Together the protocol and inclusion statement establish at least 50 distinct analyzed writers across the randomized AI modes. The exact unique analyzed-person total across days, randomized-person total, and per-arm counts are not separately reported and remain null; story and evaluation counts are not entered as people counts. Completed stories receive blinded human ratings of originality and overall creative quality, as well as computed semantic and genre similarity measures (PDF pp. 6-7, 16, 19, 21, 41). open_items.item: open_questions[0]: Exact randomized and analyzed people by arm and regression, and the flow connecting the 285-person cohort, 280 initial-survey records, and 278/271 daily stories, remain unreported (PDF pp. 11, 18-21). Author-provided assignment and analysis flow would settle these counts. This does not leave criterion 2 unclear: the one-story-per-student Day 2 protocol and inclusion of all 271 Day 2 stories already establish at least 50 analyzed writers.

open_questions[1]: Tables S4/S7 and A.3 do not state whether standard errors account for repeated ratings of a story/participant or shared evaluators (PDF pp. 23, 48, 51). The posted analysis code and linked participant/story/evaluator data would identify the variance method and allow an independent-unit analysis. This affects use of precision in pooling, not any core eligibility criterion.

open_questions[2]: Confidence-interval and significance-test procedures for semantic and genre similarity, including dependence from each story's comparison with the other stories in its condition, are unstated (PDF pp. 6-7, 15-16). Posted analysis code would settle the procedures. This affects statistical interpretation and pooling, not the output-scored outcome criterion or other eligibility criteria.

open_questions[3]: The main text, recruitment section, and Figure S1 specify 105 minutes, whereas the day-specific SI task descriptions specify 75 minutes (PDF pp. 4, 18-20). Author confirmation of the implemented protocol would settle the discrepancy. Task duration does not affect any eligibility criterion.

open_questions[4]: The saved manuscript has no printed date or arXiv/journal version identifier (PDF pp. 1, 17); its filename and file-creation metadata do not establish a publication version. Author identification of this exact manuscript revision would settle provenance. The missing version identifier does not affect the three eligibility criteria for the document screened.

Unresolved reconciliation difference studies[S1].participants.n_analyzed: the exact unique analyzed-person total across both days remains null because 285 is a participating-cohort count and observation counts do not provide a deduplicated writer total (PDF pp. 11, 18, 21). Participant identifiers and outcome inclusion in the posted data would settle the exact total. This overlaps open_questions[0] and does not affect criterion 2, whose threshold is established by the Day 2 protocol and included stories.

open_questions[5] / S1-O7: The current measure vocabulary has no exact code for cosine similarity of binary genre-category vectors. The method is settled by PDF p. 16, Figure 4B; measure remains null pending an Atlas vocabulary decision. No supplement, posted data, author response, or newer manuscript is needed to establish what was measured. The output-scored diversity outcome and all three eligibility criteria remain established.
